pnl_attribution_test_frtb_pat.text: `gamma_pnl_attribution` and `pnl_attribution_test_frtb_pat` answer different questions. The first asks how much of a P&L move came from convexity. You give it `gamma` and the realised underlying move `spot_move`, and it applies ½ · Γ · dS² to give that single component. The second, the FRTB P&L Attribution Test, asks whether a risk model's P&L tracks full-revaluation P&L well enough. You give it daily `risk_theoretical_pnl` and `hypothetical_pnl` series, and it combines a Spearman rank correlation with a volatility ratio to assign a Basel traffic-light zone. Roughly, one explains where P&L came from, and the other tests the quality of a model's P&L against a regulatory benchmark (BCBS FRTB §9.5).

explain.text: `gamma_pnl_attribution` (Gamma Pnl Attribution) calculates the convexity part of a portfolio's P&L, using the formula ½ · Γ · dS². It takes two inputs: `gamma`, the portfolio's second derivative of value with respect to the underlying (∂²V/∂S²), and `spot_move`, the realised move in the underlying. In a P&L explain, this term sits alongside the first-order delta effect and captures what a linear approximation misses when the underlying moves. Because the move is squared, the sign of the move does not affect the term; the sign of `gamma` does.

when.text:
Use `gamma_pnl_attribution` (Gamma Pnl Attribution) when you want the convexity part of a P&L move, calculated as ½ · Γ · dS².

- You have a portfolio gamma (`gamma`) and a realised underlying move (`spot_move`) and want to see how much P&L the curvature of the position contributed.
- You are splitting a P&L explanation into pieces and need the second-order, spot-driven component on its own.
- You want to see how large moves in the underlying matter because the move enters squared.
- Related: `vega_pnl_attribution` covers the volatility component (ν · dσ), so it fits if your question is about changes in volatility rather than spot.
